description: We are Informatics Engineering and Information Systems & Technology students from Institut Teknologi Bandung (ITB). We like turning real planetary data into dependable software: routing, geospatial processing, web apps and testing. We are building ARES Path, a safety-first route planner for astronauts at Jezero Crater, Mars. We are looking for teammates with GIS or remote sensing, UX design, or planetary science and geology knowledge. Curious beginners are welcome too!
summary: ARES Path is a Marswalk planning and 3D exploration tool for a simulated human mission in Jezero Crater. Mars data is abundant but scattered across portals, instruments, resolutions and file formats, so an astronaut cannot easily turn it into one answer: where should I go, and can I get back? ARES Path fuses real NASA/USGS elevation, orbital imagery, geology, CRISM mineral indicators, Perseverance traverse data and MEDA environmental history into a single map, then converts those layers into decisions. It recommends routes that balance terrain safety, time, energy and scientific value, explains why an area was avoided, and recalculates when conditions change. Its Dynamic Return-to-Safety Envelope continuously shows whether the crew can still return to the habitat with a safety reserve, and MarsWalk 3D lets the user walk the same planned route across terrain reconstructed from the same data. It matters because surface EVAs will be planned under tight margins, and decisions must be traceable to data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ARES Path turns Mars map layers into an explainable EVA plan for the western delta of Jezero Crater (77.335–77.455°E, 18.420–18.500°N).

- Map-first planner: the user picks curated science targets or drops custom checkpoints on a map with toggleable elevation, slope, hazard, geology/mineralogy, rover traverse and science layers.

- Constraint-aware routing: the user sets EVA duration, energy budget, maximum preferred slope and required return reserve. The routing engine searches a 5 m cost grid derived from terrain and returns distance, duration, elevation change, energy use and a GO/NO-GO result.

- Dynamic Return-to-Safety Envelope: at every point of the traverse, the planner shows whether the astronaut can still return to the habitat while preserving the configured reserve.

- Replanning: when the energy budget drops or a segment becomes unavailable, the route is recalculated.

- MarsWalk 3D: a third-person surface mode that shares the same mission state, route and waypoints as the 2D planner, on terrain built from the same elevation and imagery data.

- Mission Analyst (optional): a language-model assistant that explains route results, inspects selected locations and proposes mission changes. Every proposal is a preview that the backend validates and recalculates; the routing engine, not the model, is the source of all route and GO/NO-GO results.

HOW IT WORKS

A reproducible Python pipeline fetches source products from NASA and USGS, reprojects them to a common Mars equirectangular coordinate system, and derives slope, hillshade, traversability and science layers.

The production application runs on a virtual machine managed through Dokploy. A React frontend provides the map planner and MarsWalk 3D, while a FastAPI backend runs the Python routing engine, validates mission changes, and powers the optional Mission Analyst. Processed scientific datasets, map imagery and 3D terrain assets are bundled with the deployment and served from the VM.

The planner and MarsWalk 3D share the same mission state, route and waypoints. The interface adapts from 360 px phones to wide desktops, with touch and keyboard/mouse controls in MarsWalk and automatic terrain quality scaling.

BENEFITS

- One synchronized mission view instead of manually comparing disconnected maps and archives.

- Safety before distance: the shortest route is not automatically preferred.

- Explainable results: hazards and route choices are traceable to a dataset or a derivation.

- Honest uncertainty: data limits are shown to the user.

LIMITATIONS

ARES Path is a decision-support prototype, not a flight-certified navigation or life-support system. Stereo DTMs can contain artifacts and do not resolve every small rock or ledge. CRISM parameters are remote-sensing indicators, not field confirmation. MEDA data is historical context, not a weather forecast. The project is not endorsed by NASA.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React, TypeScript, Vite, OpenLayers, React Three Fiber (Three.js), Python, FastAPI, GeoTIFF raster processing, VPS and R2, pytest and browser end-to-end tests.
